title: Good Friday
hookLine: Christians remember the crucifixion, often in silence

cards: Something is missing from the church this afternoon. The altar is bare. No flowers.
In some churches the bells stay silent, and people come in without chatting and leave without a word. A wooden cross may be carried in, and one by one people walk up to it.
It's the Friday before Easter, the day Christians remember the death of Jesus. And its name, oddly, is Good Friday. Today: what is remembered, and why so much of the remembering happens in silence.

teach.b: First, the darkness. The Gospels tell how Jesus was crucified under the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, outside Jerusalem.
Matthew writes, "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." The day goes dark in the middle. Second, the cry.

teach.h: MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?
teach.b: Matthew records Jesus calling out, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" They are the opening words of Psalm 22, a lament. On the cross, he prays an old prayer of abandonment.
Christians sit with that line: the one they call God's Son, voicing the feeling of being left alone. Third, different words from different Gospels.

teach.h: INTO THY HANDS; IT IS FINISHED.
teach.b: Luke gives a quieter last word: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." John gives this: "It is finished." The Bible doesn't choose between them.
It keeps all three side by side: the cry, the trust, the ending. Fourth, the silence.

In Christian belief, Easter is coming, but the day's customs don't rush to it. Catholic churches celebrate no Mass on Good Friday; instead there is a service of the Lord's Passion and the veneration of the cross.

Orthodox Christians gather around an embroidered image of Christ's body laid in the tomb and sing laments. Some Protestant churches hold services of readings and long pauses, some ending in darkness. Why good?
Christian teaching answers with what it holds that death opened: forgiveness, and the way to Easter.
But the day itself is kept quiet, the way you stay with someone who has died before you talk about anything else.

how: On Good Friday, Christians gather to hear the passion read, pray at the cross, and keep the day quietly; Catholics have no Mass that day, and Orthodox Christians sing laments around the epitaphios, the image of Christ in the tomb.

practice: For these minutes, put the phone face down or across the room, and let the sounds around you be the only sounds.

You don't need to think about the cross unless you want to; just practice what the day teaches, staying with something hard without rushing to the next thing. If you pray, you can pray with the words from Luke: into thy hands.

wordCard.voice: Good Friday: the day Christians remember the crucifixion of Jesus, kept with bare altars, readings and silence before Easter. Today's word.

orig.note: Matthew's Greek keeps the cry in Hebrew, Eli, 'my God', then translates it. Mark 15:34 has Eloi.

carryVoice: Your line: a quiet hour. Some days are kept best with fewer words. Day seven hundred fifty.
